Formulation:
The patient, a middle-aged man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, presents with a 4–5 day history of upper respiratory tract symptoms including dry cough (with minimal sputum), runny nose, sore throat, mild ear discomfort, low-grade fever/chills, and mild shortness of breath. His chronic medical conditions and central obesity predispose him to infection and potentially more severe illness, though currently symptoms are mild to moderate and stable. Psychosocial stressors include feeling physically unwell, mild marital tension ("wife nagging"), and concerns about shortness of breath. Protective factors include insight, social support from his wife, and ongoing employment. The clinical impression is a viral upper respiratory infection, with possible early bacterial lower respiratory involvement given sputum and fevers. Lisinopril-induced cough is less likely as a primary cause. Management includes symptomatic care and standby antibiotics if symptoms worsen, emphasizing rest and hydration.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold / viral pharyngitis)
- Patient Goal(s): Recover full physical health; relieve respiratory symptoms; maintain hydration and nutrition; avoid deterioration  
- Clinical Goal(s): Symptomatic relief; prevent secondary bacterial infection; monitor for worsening signs (e.g., increased breathlessness)  
- Actions (Patient): Rest; maintain fluid intake; take Paracetamol as needed for fever/chills; monitor symptoms closely; initiate antibiotics if symptoms worsen after 24–48 hours  
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provide sick leave advice/support as appropriate; supply antibiotic prescription (Amoxicillin 1 tablet TID) for delayed use; educate patient on symptom monitoring and when to return for review; encourage smoking cessation efforts  

Secondary Problem: Early bacterial lower respiratory tract infection (bronchitis or pneumonia) (provisional, medium likelihood)
- Patient Goal(s): Prevent progression of infection; maintain health and work ability  
- Clinical Goal(s): Early recognition and treatment if bacterial infection develops; reduce complications, especially given comorbid diabetes and hypertension  
- Actions (Patient): Use prescribed antibiotics if advised; seek follow-up if symptoms worsen or fail to improve by 7 days  
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provide clear instructions for antibiotic use; arrange follow-up appointment if symptoms persist or deteriorate; assess for adjustment of diabetes/HTN management if infection impacts control  

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: Viral infections; importance of rest and hydration; signs of worsening illness; antibiotic use criteria; smoking cessation benefits  
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Increasing dyspnea; chest pain; high fever; persistent or worsening cough with sputum; confusion or altered consciousness  
- Coping Strategies: Self-monitoring of symptoms; use of over-the-counter Paracetamol; maintaining positive social support; reducing smoking with vaping device  

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Implied verbal consent during consultation  
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded  
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: None recorded  
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not applicable  
- Review Date: Patient advised to return if no improvement in 7 days; no specific review date set  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold / viral pharyngitis) — High likelihood; supported by classic symptoms and gradual onset  
- Early bacterial lower respiratory tract infection (bronchitis or pneumonia) — Medium likelihood; supported by mild sputum, shortness of breath, plus fever in context of diabetes and hypertension  
- Lisinopril-induced cough — Low to medium likelihood; patient on Lisinopril with dry cough, but infection signs make this diagnosis less probable
